title: Greedy algorithms
summary: Take the best-looking choice at every step: when that is optimal, and when it fails.

steps.title: Grab the best option now
body: A **greedy** algorithm makes the locally best choice at every step and never looks back. When it works it is simple and fast.
Making change with coins `{25, 10, 5, 1}`: always take the largest coin that still fits. Watch `left` shrink in the trace.

steps.prompt: The same greedy method with coins `{4, 3, 1}`, making 6. What does it print?
steps.explain: Greedy grabs the 4 and is then stuck with two 1s. `3 + 3` uses only two coins. Greedy is not always optimal: the DP from the last lesson is.

steps.prompt: Why does greedy change-making work for `{25, 10, 5, 1}` but not for `{4, 3, 1}`?
options: In the first set a big coin never blocks a better combination of smaller ones; in the second it can
Greedy only works when there are four coin types
The first set is sorted and the second is not
Greedy works for both; the trace had a bug
steps.explain: A greedy algorithm needs proof that the local choice is always part of some best answer. For everyday currencies that holds; for arbitrary coin sets it does not.

steps.title: Interval scheduling
body: One room, many meeting requests `(start, end)`. Fit in as many as possible.

Shortest first? Earliest start? Both can fail. The rule that is **provably optimal**: sort by **end time** and take every meeting that starts after the last chosen one ends. Finishing early leaves the most room for everything else.
`O(n log n)` for the sort, then one pass. Watch `lastEnd` move forward.

steps.prompt: Which meetings get picked? What does it print?
steps.explain: Sorted by end: 1-2, 3-4, 5-6, 2-8, 0-10. The long meetings overlap what was already chosen. Picking the earliest-starting `0-10` first would have allowed only one meeting.

steps.prompt: Does a simple greedy rule give the optimal answer?
items: fewest coins for any coin set
can you reach the end of a jump array (track the furthest reach)
best value of items in a knapsack with a weight limit (items cannot be split)

steps.prompt: Jump game: `jumps[i]` is the furthest you may jump forward from `i`. Greedily track the furthest index reachable so far.
steps.explain: If you ever stand on an index beyond the furthest reachable one, you are stuck. Otherwise extend the reach and keep going.

steps.title: Most meetings
prompt: Write `int MaxMeetings((int Start, int End)[] meetings)`: the largest number of meetings that fit in one room. A meeting may start exactly when the previous one ends.
Sort by end time and pick greedily. The tests use 200,000 meetings.
starter: int MaxMeetings((int Start, int End)[] meetings)
solution: int MaxMeetings((int Start, int End)[] meetings)
template: Dojo.Eq("one long meeting loses to three short", 3, MaxMeetings(new[] { (0, 10), (1, 2), (3, 4), (2, 8), (5, 6) }));
Dojo.Eq("back to back is allowed", 3, MaxMeetings(new[] { (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4) }));
hints: `meetings.OrderBy(m => m.End)` gives them sorted by end time.
Skip a meeting whose `Start` is before the last chosen `End`; otherwise take it.

steps.title: Jump game
prompt: You start at index 0 of `jumps`; from index `i` you may move forward up to `jumps[i]` places. Write:
- `bool CanReachEnd(int[] jumps)`: can you reach the last index?
- `int MinJumps(int[] jumps)`: the fewest jumps to reach the last index (assume it is reachable; a one-item array needs 0).
CanReachEnd(new[] { 3, 2, 1, 0, 4 })   // false: every route lands on the 0

Both are greedy and `O(n)`. For `MinJumps`, treat it like BFS in rings: track the end of the current jump's range and the furthest you could reach with one more jump; when `i` reaches the end of the range, you must jump.
hints: `MinJumps`: loop `i` up to `jumps.Length - 2`. Update `furthest`; when `i == rangeEnd`, count a jump and set `rangeEnd = furthest`.
